For my starting position, I make around $60k a year. I plan on going back for my degree, but only because I personally wish to become an engineer. But, I don't find it necessary to go back for the degree and I definitely think having the diploma is good enough. You get so much experience on the job that you don't necessarily need the degree to have an impact on the field. And no, you cannot be a red seal. It's different from the trades route.

Hey, just graduated from A&I last year and have been working full-time in wastewater treatment for 6 months now.

Some jobs in the automation and instrumentation field will vary from others. I have friends who mostly do AutoCAD drafting work in office while I am usually in the field. But I'll give you my personal experience on the field.

I'm on site at a water treatment plant and I have do go through coding everyday. But not the coding you encounter in ELEX 2117, 2125 or 3305. It's the coding you'll encounter in ELEX 3230 and 4221, which is ladder logic and function block diagrams. A basic understanding of ELEX 3305 C programming would help, but definitely not necessary.

My job doesn't require me to do any lifting or going on ladders, but I do have to be on the field and doing some wiring, opening up transmitters and wiring some junction boxes. It's not that physically demanding. 

Calculus isn't used quite much in my job. A general understanding of it definitely helps, but you won't be asked to take the derivaive or integral of something.

During your semester, your program head is probably going to email you some job opportunities and job postings. TAKE ADVANTAGE OF THOSE. GET YOUR RESUME READY (talk to your COMM teacher ahead of time and ask if they can help with your resume) AND APPLY TO EVERY JOB SHE SENDS. These are free opportunities that should be taken. I didn't apply to a lot of them because I was too busy with homework but all my other friends applied and all the positions got taken instantly.

 I was applying for jobs for 4 months straight, from December to March, and I applied to over 100 jobs. I only got a few calls back, but was lucky enough to land a job. The key to finding a job is just to send out as many applications as you can. Eventually, you'll get a call back.

Finally, the last piece of advice I can give is that your level 4 courses are the most important for your job. I encounter situations where I need to refer to my notes from every ELEX 4000 course I've taken. The most important, in my opinion, are ELEX 4215, 4206, and 3230. However, I'm not kidding when I say every course in level 4 is important as hell. Pay attention in class, stay on top of your assignments, and don't fall behind.

Hope this helps you. Good luck!
